title: Availability judgments · letter positions and causes of death

blocks.text: Do people judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind? In one test, people were asked whether English has more words that begin with **r** or more words with **r as the third letter**. In another, they were given **paired causes of death**, such as botulism versus asthma, and chose which was more frequent or more likely.
children: The question probes the **availability heuristic**: easy recall is treated as a sign of high frequency.

blocks.text: About **70%** said more words begin with r, yet words with r in the third position are actually **three times more common**. Words are easier to retrieve by first letter, so those words feel more numerous. For causes of death, many people picked the dramatic cause over the more common one such as asthma, because a botulism death can become front-page news while asthma deaths go virtually unnoticed.
children: Memorable or newsworthy does not mean common.

blocks.text: Ease of remembering serves as a cue for probability, but it is shaped by distinctiveness and emotional impact as well as by how often something really happens.

Do people rely on resemblance instead of base rates and probability rules? Participants read a description and judged occupation or category. **Robert** wears glasses, speaks quietly and reads a lot, and many people call him a **librarian** rather than a farmer, even though there are about **2.2 million farms** and only **120,000 libraries**.
children: A good fit with the stereotype pushed the base rate out of the judgment.

blocks.text: In the **lawyer-engineer problem**, the group has **70 lawyers and 30 engineers**. With no description, people correctly use the 70/30 base rate. Once **Jack** is described as conservative, careful and fond of home carpentry and math puzzles, they ignore the base rate and say he is an engineer.
children: Base rates are used when they are all there is, and dropped once a description is available.

blocks.text: In the **Linda problem**, about **82%** chose that Linda is a bank teller and active in the feminist movement over bank teller alone. Feminist bank tellers are a **subset** of bank tellers, so the combination can never be more probable than the single event.
children: The better-fitting story won over the nested-set logic of the **conjunction rule**.

title: Hospital samples · extreme proportions and sample size

blocks.text: Do people take sample size into account when judging how often extreme proportions occur? Participants compared a larger hospital with about **45 births a day** and a smaller hospital with about **15 births a day**. About half of all babies are boys, and they chose which hospital recorded more days on which **over 60% were boys**: the larger, the smaller, or about the same.
children: The question is about how often a day is extreme, not about the total number of boys born.

blocks.text: The most common answer, chosen by **56%**, was **about the same**. The correct answer is the **smaller hospital**, because small samples vary more from the true rate, so a lopsided day is more likely with 15 births than with 45. Choosing the larger hospital confuses the absolute number of boys with how often an extreme proportion occurs.
children: The common answer ignores how many births stand behind each day's percentage.

blocks.text: This is why the **law of large numbers** matters: larger groups are more representative of the population, and people tend to expect small samples to be representative too.

title: Lord and colleagues · myside bias in article evaluation

blocks.text: Does an existing opinion change how the same evidence is evaluated? **Lord and colleagues (1979)** compared people who were **in favor of capital punishment** with people who were **opposed** to it. Both groups read the same article, and the researchers measured how each participant interpreted it.
children: The only thing that differed between the groups was the readers' opinion, not the article.

blocks.text: Each side saw the article as **favorable to its own position**, focusing on information that agreed with them and disregarding the rest.
children: Identical evidence was read as support by opposite camps.

blocks.text: This is **myside bias**: generating and evaluating evidence in a way that favors one's own opinions and attitudes. It is a form of **confirmation bias**, the tendency to seek information that fits a view and overlook information that argues against it.

title: Hidden number rule · confirmation and diagnostic tests

blocks.text: Do people look for evidence that could prove their own hypothesis wrong? In the **2, 4, 6 task**, participants were told that 2, 4, 6 fits a hidden rule. Nothing varied between groups. Each participant wrote their own sets of three numbers, received feedback on whether each set fit the experimenter's rule, and then proposed the rule.
children: The task records what people choose to test, not just what they conclude.

blocks.text: The most common hypothesis was **increasing intervals of two**. People mostly tested triples that fit that idea, so they kept hearing yes. The actual rule was simply **three numbers in increasing order**.
children: Repeated yes feedback cannot separate the narrow rule from the broader one.

blocks.text: Testing only what fits a hypothesis is **confirmation bias** and keeps a too-narrow belief alive. Trying to **disconfirm** the hypothesis, by testing triples that should not fit, would reveal that the belief is wrong.

title: Jellybeans · favorable counts versus winning probability

blocks.text: Do people choose by the number of winning items or by the probability of winning? Participants could earn **one dollar** for each red jellybean they drew, up to seven dollars, and before drawing they picked between two bowls. One bowl had **1 red bean out of 10**, and the other had **7 red beans out of 100**.
children: Comparing counts and comparing ratios give opposite answers here.

blocks.text: Most participants chose the **7-out-of-100 bowl**, even though 1 in 10 is a **10%** chance and 7 in 100 is only **7%**. The larger number of red beans looks like more chances, and it draws attention away from the total number of possible draws.
children: The bigger count hides the bigger total.

blocks.text: The choice was driven by considerations other than the actual probabilities of winning.

title: Ritov and Baron · convoy rerouting and lives saved

blocks.text: Do people choose the option that saves the most lives when it requires causing harm? **Ritov and Baron (1999)** described a convoy of food trucks heading to a refugee camp during a famine. Rerouting the convoy would save **1,000 people at a second camp**, but **100 people in the first camp would die**. The measure was whether participants chose to reroute.
children: The net count favors rerouting, 1,000 minus 100 is 900 lives saved.

blocks.text: Even so, **63%** did not choose to reroute, and some would keep the original route even if only **one person** would die after the change.
children: Most refused despite the better net outcome.

blocks.text: Reluctance to cause a loss can outweigh the larger number saved elsewhere, so choices are not simply about the biggest number.

title: Tetlock and colleagues · taboo and tragic outcomes

blocks.text: How do taboo and tragic tradeoffs affect moral outrage? **Tetlock, Kristel, Elson, Green, and Lerner (2000)** crossed two kinds of tradeoff with two outcomes. In the **taboo** tradeoff, a hospital administrator must choose between saving Johnny's life, which costs one million dollars, and spending that money on other hospital needs. In the **tragic** tradeoff, two children need a liver and only one is available. Johnny was either saved or not saved, and participants rated moral outrage.
children: A taboo tradeoff sets a sacred value against a secular benefit, while a tragic tradeoff sets two sacred values against each other.

blocks.text: In the taboo tradeoff, **not saving Johnny produced much greater outrage** than saving him. In the tragic tradeoff, outrage was **similar** whether Johnny was saved or not, since either choice leaves another sacred concern unmet.
children: The effect of the decision depends on the type of value conflict, which is an **interaction**.

title: Ginges and colleagues · payment, recognition, and sacred commitments

blocks.text: How do people react to compromise deals over contested issues, and does money help? **Ginges, Atran, Medin, and Shikaki (2007)** surveyed **601 Israeli settlers, 535 Palestinian refugees, and 719 Palestinian students**. Each person responded to a **taboo** deal, a **Taboo+** deal that added one billion dollars a year for ten years, and a **symbolic** deal that added recognition and an apology. Participants were also classified as **moral absolutists** or not, and the researchers measured anger, disgust and support for violence.
children: Moral absolutists treat an issue as sacred and reject compromise regardless of benefit.

blocks.text: For moral absolutists, **adding money increased anger, disgust and support for violence**, while non-absolutists responded the other way. **Symbolic recognition** lowered anger or disgust and support for violence.
children: Money can backfire when the issue is sacred, and symbolic reciprocity can help.

title: Iranian online study · sacred values, funds, sanctions, and energy results

blocks.text: Do incentives or sanctions make Iranians who hold a sacred value more willing to give up the nuclear program? **Dehghani, Atran, and colleagues (2010)** and **Dehghani, Iliev, and colleagues (2009)** ran an online study in a **2 x 3 design**: program type (energy or weapons) by deal type. The **Taboo** deal was the baseline, **Taboo+** added 40 billion dollars, and **Taboo-** added the threat of sanctions. Participants rated personal approval, the anger they expected if the government approved, and whether the deal seemed misleading.
children: A sacred-value response meant giving up the program should not be done no matter how great the consequences.

blocks.text: Only about **14%** (energy) and **13%** (weapons) gave that response. In the energy condition, those participants showed **lower approval** with funds or sanctions than with the basic deal, and anticipated anger was **highest with funds**. Participants without a sacred value gave higher approval and lower anger, with little change across deals.
children: For a sacred commitment, improving the financial terms does not make a deal more acceptable.
